Title:
Editorial: Coarse graining in quantum gravity -- Bridging the gap between microscopic models and spacetime physics
Authors:
Astrid Eichhorn
,
Benjamin Bahr
,
Antonio D. Pereira
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract:
The Renormalization Group encodes three concepts that could be key to accelerate progress in quantum gravity. First, it provides a micro-macro connection that could connect microscopic spacetime physics to phenomenology at observationally accessible scales. Second, it enables a search for universality classes that could link diverse quantum-gravity approaches and allow us to discover that distinct approaches could encode the same physics in mathematically distinct structures. Third, it enables the emergence of symmetries at fixed points of the Renormalization Group flow, providing a way for spacetime symmetries to emerge from settings in which these are broken at intermediate steps of the construction. These three concepts make the Renormalization Group an attractive method and conceptual underpinning of quantum gravity. Yet, in its traditional setup as a local coarse-graining, it could appear at odds with concepts like background independence that are expected of quantum gravity. Within the last years, several approaches to quantum gravity have found ways how these seeming contradictions could be reconciled and the power of the Renormalization Group approach unleashed in quantum gravity. This special issue brings together research papers and reviews from a broad range of quantum gravity approaches, providing a partial snapshot of this evolving field.

Title:
Extra cost of erasure due to quantum lifetime broadening
Authors:
Joe Dunlop
,
Federico Cerisola
,
Juliette Monsel
,
Sofia Sevitz
,
Jorge Tabanera-Bravo
,
Jonathan Dexter
,
Federico Fedele
,
Natalia Ares
,
Janet Anders
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract:
The energy cost of erasing a bit of information was fundamentally lower bounded by Landauer, in terms of the temperature of its environment: $W\geq k_\mathrm{B} T \ln 2$. However, in real electronic devices, the information-bearing system is usually in contact with two or more electrodes, with different temperatures and chemical potentials. It is not clear what sets the cost of erasure in such nonequilibrium situations. One promising technology for testing the thermodynamic limits of information processing is quantum dots, in which a bit is encoded in the presence or absence of a single electron. We here develop a thermodynamic description of devices of this type and find that, in addition to the electrode temperatures, the potential difference across the quantum dot and lifetime broadening of its energy level contribute to the minimum work cost of erasure. In practical contexts, these contributions may significantly outweigh the cost due to temperature alone.

article.body:
Research teams have been mapping how physical systems hold traces of their history, specifically looking at causal memory. This means a system’s present state helps predict future outcomes. Researchers used coarse-graining, which is an analogy like looking at a pointillist painting from across the room where individual dots blur into a coherent shape, to simplify complex systems and study their memory. Recent readings suggest that this process of simplifying information fundamentally limits how accurately we can reconstruct a system's history. It turns out that maintaining reliable memory is not free; it requires specific energy inputs, and there is a direct trade-off between the precision of the record and the energy the system loses during the process. Some interpretations suggest this link is universal for physical systems, while others argue it depends heavily on how the system is driven by outside forces [1]. Our focus shifted to how these individual memories become public facts, or objective records. An objective record is one that many independent observers can agree upon, regardless of their own viewpoint. To understand this, imagine a news broadcast reaching thousands of listeners; the information is the same for everyone, regardless of where they are standing. Researchers found that this reliability comes from redundancy, where the environment copies a system's state into multiple, independent parts. This ensures the information is robust, meaning it does not vanish easily. We looked at how this happens even when quantum scrambling tries to hide or delocalize information across a system. The records persist because of specific patterns called spectrum broadcast structures, which effectively lock that information into the surrounding environment [2]. Finally, the group investigated whether chemistry itself acts as a memory device. They studied autocatalytic networks, which are chemical systems that sustain themselves. An analogy is a chain reaction where the products of a chemical step act as catalysts to speed up the creation of more of those same products, allowing the system to keep running. Researchers are using algebraic math to look at stoichiometric submatrices, essentially grids representing the proportions of ingredients, to see if these networks can hold stable, history-dependent states without modern DNA. The findings suggest that these systems might hit a threshold where simple chemical persistence turns into something resembling heredity, but this remains theoretical. The distinction between simple state-holding and true template-copying is still a major point of discussion within our group, as we struggle to verify if these theoretical patterns hold up in active flow-reactor experiments [3]. This leaves us with a persistent uncertainty: At what precise threshold does a system shift from merely holding a history to actively creating a lineage that can adapt?

Summary

Our group examined how physical systems keep records of the past. We found that simplifying a system to understand it usually costs energy and limits accuracy. We also studied how information spreads through an environment so that many people can see the same facts, even when the system is jumbled. Finally, we looked at chemical networks that act like a self-sustaining loop. While these systems can remember their own history, we still do not know exactly when they cross the line into becoming capable of evolving.
article.lede: Our latest research explores the physical limits of memory storage, how information becomes publicly accessible, and whether chemical networks can sustain historical records.
article.lens: This checkpoint synthesizes research on the energetic cost of memory, the emergence of objective facts via environmental redundancy, and the potential for autocatalytic chemical networks to function as primitive hereditary systems.
article.title: Progress in Mapping Physical, Objective, and Chemical Memory

actions.findings:
Entropy production in driven overdamped Langevin systems can be effectively upper-bounded by the statistics of driven particles alone, with passive degrees of freedom contributing to reduced dissipation. [peer-30b9153ce0fe31018c8e3730]

Non-reciprocal couplings in autonomous information engines can significantly modulate inter-dot information flow, potentially optimizing energy conversion efficiency. [peer-f3ee30889b8396e02ea0588a]
actions.limitations: Current findings rely primarily on overdamped Langevin models and autonomous double-quantum-dot architectures; high-inertia regimes and fully non-Markovian dynamics remain speculative.
actions.next_questions: Determine if the thermodynamic benefits of non-reciprocal coupling generalize to larger networks of coupled information processors.
actions.reason: Incorporating recent peer-reviewed bounds on entropy production and non-reciprocal coupling dynamics to refine the project's understanding of dissipation.
actions.summary: This revision synthesizes findings on entropy production bounds and the role of non-reciprocal couplings in autonomous information engines, establishing that predictive information and passive degrees of freedom provide concrete upper bounds on dissipation in driven systems.
